solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique, linked answer split by the grid); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Maiden is full of anger, things being not what they seem to be

definitions.text: things being not what they seem to be

parts.note: M is the cricket abbreviation for a maiden over

indicators.note: being full of something means holding it, so the word is wraps round the next piece

parts.note: anger means rage

explanation.surface: A young woman so furious that the world around her seems unreal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Maiden' suggests a girl, but in cricket it is a maiden over, abbreviated M.
explanation.definitionFit: Illusions seen in hot deserts are the classic example of things that are not really there.

clue.text: Friend full of nostalgia surprisingly for Mississippi

indicators.note: a friend full of something holds it inside, so the friend word wraps round the rest

parts.note: mate is British slang for friend

indicators.note: surprisingly signals the letters of nostalgia come out in an unexpected order

explanation.surface: A pal is overcome with homesick longing for the Deep South.
explanation.walkthrough: 'surprisingly' rearranges the clue's own word nostalgia into GNOLIASTA, the middle of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The nickname of the US state Mississippi comes from its magnolia trees, its state flower.

clue.text: Ref initially enrages football team

indicators.note: initially picks out the first letter of the word Ref

parts.note: enrages means makes angry, angers

explanation.surface: A referee's early decision infuriates the players of one club.
explanation.walkthrough: RANGERS is a Glasgow football club (also Queens Park Rangers in London).
explanation.definitionFit: Rangers is the name of a well-known Scottish football club, so it names a team.

clue.text: See 15
Nice lass arranged plants

indicators.note: arranged signals the letters of Nice lass are set out in a new order

explanation.surface: A pleasant girl has done the flower arranging.
explanation.definitionFit: Sanicles are woodland herbs of the carrot family, so they are a kind of plant.

clue.text: Plant donkey found by East Anglian river

indicators.note: found by means placed next to, so the river comes before the donkey

parts.note: the Cam is the river flowing through Cambridge in East Anglia
an ass is a donkey

explanation.surface: A donkey turns up beside a river in eastern England.
explanation.walkthrough: East Anglia is the eastern bulge of England (Norfolk, Suffolk, Cambridgeshire).
explanation.definitionFit: Camass is a North American plant of the lily family with edible bulbs.

clue.text: Cross put above cathedral city in an attractive way

indicators.note: in a down answer, the piece put above comes first

parts.note: to cross a line or path is to cut across it
Ely is a small cathedral city in Cambridgeshire

explanation.surface: A crucifix is placed above an English cathedral city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cross' looks like a crucifix but is the verb meaning cut.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something prettily or charmingly is doing it in a cute manner.

clue.text: A super tom around? Maybe this isn't needed then!

definitions.text: A super tom around? Maybe this isn't needed then!

indicators.note: around signals the letters of A super tom are turned about into a new order

explanation.surface: With a champion cat on the prowl, you can skip the mousing gadget.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition: with a brilliant mouser about, a trap for mice is redundant.
explanation.definitionFit: A spring device for catching mice is pointless when a good cat keeps them down.

clue.text: Endless expertise shown with two newspapers presenting winter sports feature

indicators.note: endless means the last letter is removed

parts.note: expertise means skill
the i and the FT (Financial Times) are two British newspapers

explanation.surface: Know-how covered in a couple of papers presents a feature on winter sports.
explanation.walkthrough: The i is a British daily paper; FT is the Financial Times.
explanation.definitionFit: A cable lift carrying people up a slope is standard equipment at a ski resort.

clue.text: Biscuit with rotten egg in — nasty turn ensues

indicators.note: ensues means comes after, so the second piece follows the first
rotten signals the letters of egg in are spoiled into a new order
nasty signals the letters of turn are mangled

explanation.surface: A cookie with a bad egg in it, and a nasty stomach upset follows.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rotten' makes GINGE from EGG IN; 'nasty' makes RNUT from TURN.
explanation.definitionFit: A ginger nut is a hard ginger-flavoured British biscuit, a cookie in American terms.

clue.text: Old soldier in sixties show suitable for kids making comeback

indicators.note: making a comeback means coming back, so the pieces are read backwards

parts.note: Hair is the 1960s rock musical
U is the British film certificate for universal viewing, fine for children

explanation.surface: A family-friendly 1960s show is being revived.
explanation.walkthrough: 'making comeback' turns HAIRU round. U is the British film rating for all ages.
explanation.definitionFit: Uriah the Hittite was the Old Testament soldier whom King David sent to die in battle.

clue.text: 3D show of yesteryear?

definitions.meaning: 3d is three old pence in pre-decimal British money, half of a six-penny coin
a 1963 West End musical starring Tommy Steele

explanation.surface: A three-dimensional show from years gone by.
explanation.walkthrough: '3D' looks like three-dimensional, but d was the symbol for an old British penny, so 3d is threepence.
explanation.definitionFit: Threepence is half the old silver coin worth six pennies, and the phrase is also an old musical's title.

clue.text: Work of poet being performed in cinema?

parts.note: an ode is a lyric poem
a play that is on is being performed

explanation.surface: A poet's work being staged in a picture house.
explanation.definitionFit: Odeon is the name of a long-running British chain of picture houses.

clue.text: Scottish island, say — one with a learner in an academic setting

parts.note: Coll is an island of the Inner Hebrides
say means for example, e.g.
I is the Roman numeral one
L is the learner driver's plate

explanation.surface: A Hebridean island, for instance, where someone takes a learner to school.
explanation.definitionFit: Collegial describes what belongs to a college, a university or academic body.

clue.text: Enticers manoeuvring without anybody seeing

indicators.note: manoeuvring signals the letters of Enticers are moved about

explanation.surface: Tempters scheming where nobody can watch.
explanation.definitionFit: Done privately or covertly, out of public view, is an idiom for something hidden from witnesses.

clue.text: Scientist in den with container for absorbing nitrogen

indicators.note: absorbing means taking in, so the pieces around take the nitrogen symbol into them

parts.note: a den is a cave, an animal's lair
a dish is a container
N is the chemical symbol for nitrogen

explanation.surface: A scientist in a lab uses a vessel to absorb nitrogen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for absorbing' lets the den and the container together take in the nitrogen, which lands at their join.
explanation.definitionFit: Henry Cavendish was the 18th-century English chemist who discovered hydrogen.

clue.text: Unruly gang re-enter border village

indicators.note: unruly signals the letters of gang re-enter are run wild into a new order

explanation.surface: A rowdy gang comes back into a village at the frontier.
explanation.walkthrough: GRETNA GREEN is a Scottish village just over the border from England, famous for runaway weddings.
explanation.definitionFit: The village lies on the Scotland-England boundary, so it is literally a frontier settlement.

clue.text: Conservative wanting capital punishment is coming to different view

parts.note: hanging is a form of execution

explanation.surface: A Tory who supports the death penalty is having second thoughts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wanting' is a link word here, though it reads as desiring.
explanation.definitionFit: Altering one's opinion, moving to another view, is a sense of shifting position.

clue.text: Servant of broadcaster appearing around 4 to 5

indicators.note: around means the broadcaster's name goes about the numerals

parts.note: Sky is a British satellite broadcaster
IV is the Roman numeral four
V is the Roman numeral five

explanation.surface: A broadcaster's domestic help appears in the late afternoon.
explanation.walkthrough: '4 to 5' looks like a time of day but is two Roman numerals in a row. A skivvy is a British word for a menial housemaid.
explanation.definitionFit: A skivvy is a lowly domestic drudge, someone hired to do the household chores.

clue.text: Trendy present maybe making one passionate

parts.note: in means fashionable
the present is an example of a grammatical tense

explanation.surface: A fashionable gift could make someone ardent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'present' looks like a gift, but it is the grammatical tense.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone with strong, fervent feelings is described with this synonym of ardent.

clue.text: Fellow going to room cut bread

parts.note: chap means a fellow

indicators.note: cut means shortened, losing the last letter

parts.note: an attic is a room in the roof

explanation.surface: A man heads into a room to slice the loaf.
explanation.definitionFit: Chapatti is an unleavened Indian flatbread.

clue.text: Hot air from the group believing everything — almost everything

parts.note: the Royal Marines, RM, from the idiom 'tell it to the marines', said of those who will swallow any tall story

indicators.note: almost means the last letter is dropped

parts.note: everything means all

explanation.surface: Nonsense spouted by a credulous group, ending in near-totality.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hot air' suggests empty talk, but here it is rising warm air. 'Tell it to the marines' is an old British saying implying marines believe anything.
explanation.definitionFit: A rising current of warm air, used by gliders and birds, is this meteorological term.

clue.text: Load of lies in paper

definitions.meaning: a ... of lies is an idiom for a whole web of falsehoods
thin soft paper for wiping or wrapping

explanation.surface: A pack of untruths printed in a newspaper.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom 'a tissue of lies' and a soft paper handkerchief share the same word.

clue.text: What a lecturer wants to be paid?

definitions.text: What a lecturer wants to be paid?

parts.words: What a lecturer wants to be paid?
parts.note: the surface suggests a fee, but what is paid to a speaker is heed, as in the idiom about listening

explanation.surface: A speaker hoping for a decent fee.
explanation.walkthrough: 'paid' suggests money, but the idiom is to pay heed to a speaker.
explanation.definitionFit: Listeners pay heed to a lecturer; the idiom pairs the verb 'pay' with this word.

clue.text: Strips, having returned for rest

indicators.note: returned means turned back, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: to strip skin off is to peel; strips means peels

explanation.surface: Someone takes their clothes off after coming home, ready for a lie-down.
explanation.definitionFit: Slumber is the deepest kind of rest.

clue.text: Groovy dude

definitions.meaning: a dandy, a fashionably dressed man

explanation.definitionFit: Both an old-fashioned word for 'great' and a noun for a smartly dressed toff.

clue.text: Boredom with EU in Britain finally resolved?

indicators.note: resolved suggests a sorting out, so the letters are put into a new order
finally picks out the last letter of Britain

explanation.surface: The tedium of the EU question in Britain finally being settled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'resolved' rearranges EUIN and N.
explanation.definitionFit: Ennui is a French-derived word for listless weariness and tedium.

clue.text: Cartoon character on the web?

parts.note: the surface suggests someone famous online, but this comic hero literally swings on webs he spins

explanation.surface: A cartoon figure who is popular on the internet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'web' suggests the internet, but the hero spins real webs.
explanation.definitionFit: The Marvel superhero shoots and swings on spider silk, so he is literally on a web.

clue.text: He may get involved with IT etc with no end of excitement

definitions.text: He may get involved with IT etc with no end of excitement

indicators.note: get involved signals the letters are tangled together into a new order
end of picks out the last letter of excitement, which is taken away

explanation.surface: A computer enthusiast gets wrapped up in technology without much thrill.
explanation.walkthrough: HE plus ITETC, with T (end of 'excitement') taken out, is rearranged; 'with no' signals the removal.
explanation.definitionFit: A computer specialist or tech enthusiast is informally called by this word.

clue.text: High wind besetting one lake gone finally — this one?

indicators.note: besetting means surrounding, so the wind word goes around the next pieces

parts.note: a gale is a high wind
I is the Roman numeral one

indicators.note: finally picks out the last letter of gone

explanation.surface: A storm surrounds a lake that has vanished.
explanation.walkthrough: 'this one?' points back to 'lake': the Sea of Galilee is a lake in Israel.
explanation.definitionFit: The Sea of Galilee is in fact a freshwater lake, so it is one lake the clue could mean.
